title: Pinchas: the five sisters (Numbers 27:1–11)
hook: Zelophehad's daughters ask to inherit; God tells Moses they speak right
tomorrow: Pinchas: a shepherd for the flock

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pinchas, the zealot, was given a covenant of peace, and the word peace is written in the scroll with a broken letter. Your line was peace is written broken. Did you soften one fire? Day four hundred sixty-seven.

A rule that has always been the rule, and it leaves someone out. It's easy to grumble about a rule like that at the kitchen table and leave it there. The people are counted again, family by family, to divide the land they're about to enter. The land will pass from fathers to sons. And then five women walk up to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting and stand in front of Moses, Eleazar the priest, the chiefs and the entire community. Their names are Mahlah, Noa, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah. Their father, Zelophehad, had no sons.
screen: `A RULE THAT LEAVES YOU OUT.` → `FIVE WOMEN AT THE TENT.` → `THEIR FATHER HAD NO SONS.`

segments.voice: Here's what they say, in paraphrase. Our father died in the wilderness. He wasn't part of Korach's rebellion; he died in his own sin. And he had no sons. Why should our father's name disappear from his family just because he had no son? Give us a holding among our father's brothers. Notice how carefully they argue. They aren't asking for themselves first; they're asking that their father's name not be erased. They head off the obvious objection: he wasn't a rebel. And they make the request in public, before every authority at once. Moses doesn't answer. He brings their case before God. And God says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right." Give them their father's inheritance. Then something bigger happens. The answer becomes a law for everyone: if a man dies without a son, his inheritance passes to his daughter. Five women standing at a tent changed the law for every family after them. The rabbis admired them enormously. The Talmud calls them wise, skilled at reading the law, and righteous, and says they chose their moment carefully, speaking when the subject of inheritance was already on the table. Some sages added that this passage of the Torah was meant to be written through them all along, as if God had been waiting for someone to ask. The daughters' names appear several times in the Bible, and they aren't always listed in the same order. One teaching reads that as a sign that all five were equal.
screen: `DON'T LET OUR FATHER'S NAME DISAPPEAR.` · `MOSES BRINGS IT BEFORE GOD.` · `THE DAUGHTERS SPEAK RIGHT.` · `ONE QUESTION, A LAW FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for what's fair. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing in your life that feels unfair and that you've only complained about privately. A workload, a family arrangement, a policy. Now imagine standing at the tent like the five sisters. How would you put it, calmly and clearly? Who would you ask, and when would be the right moment? Find the first sentence, the one that names what's fair without attacking anyone. Hold it gently until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Pinchas. The portion where five sisters ask to inherit, and God tells Moses: the daughters of Zelophehad speak right.
Your line: the daughters speak right. Today, make one fair request out loud, to the person who can actually say yes. Day four hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: The daughters of Zelophehad are read in the portion of Pinchas each summer, and their names, Mahlah, Noa, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, are named in full each time the story is read.

fork.setup: you're one of five sisters. the law gives land only to sons, and your father had none. what do you do?
options: stand before Moses and the whole community and ask.
fork.reveal: they asked, in public, at the Tent of Meeting. God said they speak right, and the law changed for every family.

original.note: Hebrew: the daughters of Zelophehad speak right (Numbers 27:7).

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about property.
what it means: five women ask, in public, for what's fair, and their question becomes a law for everyone.
what a scholar hears: Bava Batra 119b calls them wise, interpreters of the law and righteous; Sifrei says the passage was meant to be written through them.
recall: a law with no stated reason

sources.quoted: The daughters of Zelophehad speak right

sources.ref: Sifrei Bamidbar on Numbers 27:5; Rashi on Numbers 27:1, 27:5

notes: Numbers 27:7 JPS 1917 'The daughters of Zelophehad speak right'; confirm.
Bava Batra 119b (wise, expounders, righteous; spoke at the proper time) and Sifrei/Rashi on 27:5 (passage fit to be written through them); confirm.
The varying order of the sisters' names (Numbers 27:1 vs 36:11) and the teaching that they were equal (Bava Batra 120a); confirm reference.
The hook's census reference is to Numbers 26.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the paraphrase of 27:3 had added 'like many in that generation', which the sisters don't say; cut. Hook no longer opens with 'most people grumble' or tells the listener a rule leaves them out; howItsDone no longer claims the names are 'often taught to children as heroes'.
